title: Why does gold still matter?
seoTitle: Why Gold Still Matters: Central Banks, Inflation and Safe-Haven Demand
seoDescription: Learn why gold still matters in modern markets, what drives its price, why central banks hold it, and what risks investors should understand.
excerpt: Gold remains a globally recognized reserve asset shaped by interest rates, currencies, central-bank demand and periods of uncertainty.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: Gold has no cash flow, but its scarcity and long history as a monetary asset support global demand.
Real interest rates and the U.S. dollar can influence gold because they change the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.
Central banks hold gold as part of reserve diversification.
Gold can be volatile and should not be treated as a guaranteed hedge against every crisis or inflation episode.
body: Gold has played a monetary role for thousands of years, yet it still appears in modern central-bank reserves and investment portfolios. That can seem strange in a world of electronic payments and digital assets.
Its continued relevance comes from a combination of scarcity, global recognition, limited credit risk and the fact that it is not issued by a company or government.

sections.heading: Why gold is different from stocks and bonds
paragraphs: A stock can produce profits and dividends. A bond promises interest and principal payments. Gold does neither. Its value depends on what buyers are willing to pay for the metal itself.
That makes gold sensitive to macroeconomic conditions rather than company earnings. Investors often compare its appeal with the returns available on cash and bonds.

sections.heading: The role of real interest rates
paragraphs: Because gold does not pay interest, higher real yields can increase the opportunity cost of holding it. When inflation-adjusted bond yields are low or falling, gold may become relatively more attractive.
The relationship is important but not mechanical. Geopolitical risk, currency moves and central-bank buying can push gold in other directions.

sections.heading: Why the dollar matters
paragraphs: Gold is commonly priced internationally in U.S. dollars. A stronger dollar can make gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies, while a weaker dollar can have the opposite effect.
Dollar moves are only one input, but they are closely watched by commodity traders and macro investors.

sections.heading: Why central banks hold gold
paragraphs: Central banks hold reserves to support financial stability, confidence and external payments. Those reserves often include foreign currencies, government bonds and gold.
Gold can provide diversification because it is not a liability of another government. That feature can become more attractive when geopolitical or sanctions risk is a concern.

sections.heading: Is gold an inflation hedge?
paragraphs: Gold is often described as an inflation hedge, but the relationship depends heavily on the time horizon and economic environment. Gold can rise during inflationary periods, but it can also underperform when real yields rise strongly.
It is more useful to think of gold as a scarce macro asset influenced by inflation expectations, rates, currencies and risk sentiment rather than as a perfect one-variable hedge.

sections.heading: The main risks
paragraphs: Gold prices can fall sharply and can remain weak for long periods. Physical ownership introduces storage and transaction costs, while financial products add their own fees and structural considerations.
Gold therefore has a role in some portfolios, but its historical reputation should not be confused with certainty of return.

faq.question: Why do central banks buy gold?
faq.answer: Gold can diversify reserves and is not a liability of another country or issuer.

faq.question: Does gold always rise when inflation rises?
faq.answer: No. Real interest rates, the dollar, risk sentiment and central-bank demand can all influence gold at the same time.

faq.question: Does gold pay interest?
faq.answer: No. Physical gold does not produce interest or dividends.
